title: CAT: Interpretable Concept-based Taylor Additive Models

problem.claim: Feature-based generalized additive models require many parameters, are prone to overfitting, are difficult to train and scale, and become less interpretable for humans on datasets with many features.

gap.claim: Existing concept-based interpretable methods require extensive domain-expert annotation of concept names and ground-truth values.

contributions.claim: CAT is an interpretable concept-based Taylor additive model that simplifies concept-based explanation without requiring expert concept annotations.

CAT groups input features, embeds each group into a one-dimensional high-level concept representation, and processes those representations with a white-box Taylor Neural Network using polynomial relationships.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe CAT as a novel interpretable concept-based Taylor additive model.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Across multiple benchmarks, CAT reportedly outperforms or competes with baselines while using fewer extensive model parameters.
CAT reportedly explains model predictions effectively through high-level concepts.

narrative_sequence.summary: Generalized Additive Models use neural networks to learn feature-wise nonlinear functions combined by a linear model for prediction.
Feature-based GAM explanations face parameter, overfitting, scalability, and human-interpretability limitations, while concept-based methods impose extensive expert-labeling requirements.
CAT avoids expert concept annotations by using user-defined broad feature groups, one-dimensional concept representations, and a polynomial Taylor Neural Network.
The authors report competitive or superior benchmark performance, reduced parameter requirements, and effective high-level concept explanations.
The abstract states that source code is available.

source_observation.claim: Broad user-provided feature groups can replace extensive expert annotation while supporting high-level concept representations.

interpretation.claim: Interpretability workflows may reduce annotation cost by shifting from precise concept labels to lightweight feature organization.

application.claim: For high-dimensional tabular modeling, begin with metadata-based feature grouping and evaluate whether grouped representations preserve useful explanatory structure.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that broad grouping is sufficient across domains or that it preserves explanation quality under all feature configurations.

unknowns: The specific benchmarks, baselines, metrics, and comparison conditions are not reported.
The magnitude of parameter reduction and performance differences is not reported.
The procedure and quality criteria for selecting feature groups are not reported.
Training details, computational costs, and limitations are not reported.
